entries.title: The book’s calm-place idea near age three
entries.summary: Davies describes a child-chosen calm place near age three. Her prose says around 3, while the recap says over 3; this is not a setup instruction for every child in the 2–3-year band.
detail: The idea is attributed to Jane Nelsen. In Davies’s description, a child chooses whether to use the space and how long to stay. It is never a threat or an imposed time-out, and an adult can offer to go along.

The prose and recap also describe suggesting more time there if a child remains upset. That sits within the wider guidance to stay available, offer rather than insist on touch, and act immediately to stop harm. It does not make comfort conditional on being calm.

For the toddler years, Davies’s recurring sequence is support through the feeling, reconnection after calm, and help making amends when needed. The differing calm-place ages should not become a reason to send a younger child away.

qualifications: Offer rather than assume a cuddle; if pushed away, ensure safety and remain available.
In public, move out of the way if possible and allow time; the purpose is not to speed up or distract away the emotion.
She disagrees with ignoring a tantrum and uses an adult friendship analogy to explain connection.
If time requires leaving, she describes gentle help and factual narration; her45-minute example is not a prescribed waiting duration.
The summary138 additionally suggests rubbing a back/singing if accepted, standing nearby, and separating children when needed for safety.

The anticipatory list on138 identifies source possibilities, not certain motives or an exhaustive diagnosis of a particular tantrum; avoidance is qualified by if possible and does not promise prevention.

qualifications: Examples include heat, outlets, road access, going too far unattended and climbing by windows.
If the child returns repeatedly, consider changing access or removing the hazard.
The source’s box-over-outlet, couch-before-wires and locked-room cabinet examples lack implementation specifications; they are not blanket home-safety approvals.

qualifications: The child need not accept contact; reconnection precedes repair.

qualifications: Examples include collecting thrown items, cleaning wall marks, fixing a toy, checking the other child, fetching a tissue and asking if the child wants to apologize.
Adults can help with repair; rushing it before calm invites resistance.
Avoid forced, sarcastic or meaningless apologies; adult mistakes toward their own child also offer opportunities to model amends.
The later-child breakfast anecdote is illustrative context, not a toddler cooking task.
